title: Out of The Woods
reviewNotes: Reconstructed the six-piece position after ...Rxd8 and Ke7, preserving Black’s pawn on d5. Checked source rook sacrifice and resulting winning pawn ending; independently added losing ...Ra8/b6 and White’s losing premature promotion after ...Ra8, explicitly labeled. Earlier eight-piece setup remains context. Rxd8 in the independent line is not check.
transcript: Fools would resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius [music] would be able to find the incredible win in this position. White is left with only three pawns against one pawn, one rook, and one bishop, and it seems like he's completely lost because it is black to move. So, black can give a check on C5, make the king move, and then save the rook. And now all the promotions are stopped, but white knows just how hard it is to stop two connected passers. So, he plays pawn to C7. And now these two pawns are ready to help each other to promote. But black is not just going to sit back and watch while white promotes. He can play bishop to B6 and now prepare to meet the promotion to a new queen with a capture from the rook. And after white recaptures and promotes, he would be able to take again, and this would actually be completely winning for black. But of course, the D pawn is not the only pawn that can promote in this position. And indeed, the correct move is to promote the C pawn. And now if black was to recapture like this, white would be able to recapture, promote, and win the game. But black is not that naive, and he comes up with a surprising resource, the very precise bishop to D8, setting up a mating net. If white ignores the threat and for example pushes the pawn, rook to F6 would be a checkmate. There are no safe checks with the white queen, and if the king moves, this is still going to be a checkmate. So, is this it? Is black simply out of the woods in this position? Well, not exactly. White has the majestic and brilliant queen takes D8, sacrificing the newly born queen because of course, after rook takes, he can play king to E7, attacking the black rook, and preparing to promote a new queen, and then running with the other pawn to another promotion. But you see, for once, black is actually out of the woods because incredibly he has a counter brilliancy. The beautiful rook takes D7 sacrificing the rook for the pawn because after king to C5 the white pawn is under attack. If you push it, I'm going to take it and then run to promotion and the white king is simply too far away to defend the pawn. This would still allow the capture and the promotion and black is going to win this game.
